subject: mixed species groups and different detection sources

messages.author: e063c2b8771183d2
messages.subject: mixed species groups and different detection sources
parts:
Dear list members,

I would be grateful if someone could give me some light in 2 distance =
sampling related issues.

For primate surveys in the Amazonian forests is quite usual to detect =
some species, e.g. Capuchin Monkeys, sometimes visualy and in other =
instances through auditory cues. Should this sightings be stratified for =
different detenction function curves?

Another thing, perhaps a little more complex: some of this Capuchin =
Monkey groups are eventually detected through auditory cues given by an =
associated species of monkey, the Squirrel Monkey, which in turn is also =
being surveyed. Therefore detection of one species influences detection =
of another. The opposite relation is also true, but not so frequent. =
Should those be also stratified? What would be the best approach?

Thanks,

Leonardo Fleck

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: mixed species groups and different detection sources
parts:
> > I would be grateful if someone could give me some light in 2 distance sampling related issues.
> >
> > For primate surveys in the Amazonian forests is quite usual to detect some species, e.g. Capuchin Monkeys, sometimes visualy and in other instances through auditory cues. Should this sightings be stratified for different detenction function curves?
> >
> > Another thing, perhaps a little more complex: some of this Capuchin Monkey groups are eventually detected through auditory cues given by an associated species of monkey, the Squirrel Monkey, which in turn is also being surveyed. Therefore detection of one species influences detection of another. The opposite relation is also true, but not so frequent. Should those be also stratified? What would be the best approach?

Probably in both cases, it is worth using the MCDS engine of Distance 4,
with cue type as a factor. Then look at the fitted detection functions
and use the goodness-of-fit statistics to assess whether you have a good
fit for each cue type. In fact, pooling robustness means that the
standard approach will probably work OK, provided the detection functions
for different cue types are not too extreme. You could try analyses with
and without cue type as a factor to check this.

Steve
